evidence.quote: An 84-year-old male was admitted to our hospital with a compression fracture. Because the patient’s condition deteriorated during admission, a CVC was required for critical care. It was initially planned for insertion into the right subclavian vein, but the clinician realized that it had inadvertently been inserted into an artery, and removal was consulted 21 hours after the insertion. Chest radiography revealed that the CVC, which was intended to follow the path of the subclavian vein, was crossing over the trachea (Fig. 1A).
A. Chest radiograph after CVC insertion shows the catheter crossing the midline (arrowheads) with pneumonia.

A 60-year-old male with inadvertent common carotid artery cannulation treated with a vascular plug.A. Chest radiograph after CVC insertion shows that the abnormal position of the catheter (arrowheads) deviating towards the contralateral side, indicating arterial cannulation.B. A venogram was performed via the right internal jugular vein to estimate the distance between the venous exit and arterial entry points (Fig. 2D). The length was measured to be 45 mm, which is within the suitable range for plug use. Performing balloon tamponade on the proximal right SCA can temporarily occludes the right vertebral artery; therefore, the Headhunter catheter was repositioned for a left vertebral angiogram to evaluate the cerebral posterior circulation. Both vertebral arteries were normal. Thus, it was determined that the temporary occlusion of the right vertebral artery would not pose a risk of brain ischemia. After changing the Headhunter catheter to a 7-Fr sheath, a 12 mm × 40 mm balloon catheter was placed and inflated in the proximal right SCA.

Simultaneously, the CVC was replaced with a 5-Fr Impress catheter. A 6 mm type IV Amplatzer Vascular Plug was deployed for tract embolization (Fig. 2E). After 3 minutes of inflation, angiography of the right brachiocephalic artery revealed no extravasation (Fig. 2F). After the procedure, ultrasonography was performed to assess the relationship between the vascular plug and vein (Fig. 2G). The procedure was completed without complications, and no neurological deficits were observed during the 7-day hospitalization period. A follow-up visit 3 weeks later revealed no abnormalities.
